fluvial-environments: At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?

On 23 December 2013, 43–45 mm of rain fell on two river basins in southern England. Within a day, one river surged to one of its highest flows since records began; the other barely rose, and peaked only in mid-February after weeks more rain. Why did the same storm have such different effects?
A silt grain is one-hundredth the width of a coarse sand grain, yet water must flow about three times as fast to pick it up. Why?
Niagara Falls has moved about 7 miles (11 km) upstream in about 12,000 years. How does a waterfall move backwards?
A study found that urbanisation made Hurricane Harvey-scale flooding in Houston's basins about 21 times as likely in 2017. How can a city make a flood worse?
In 1995, more than 250,000 people in the Netherlands had to leave their homes as the rivers rose. The Dutch response was not simply higher dikes. What did they do?
A whole winter's rain fell on land barely above the sea. Why did the water stay for months?
ecosystems: Tundra and hot desert both get very little rain, yet they look nothing alike. What sorts the world's biomes?
Tundra and grassland are both treeless and both have cold winters. Why is only one soil so fertile?
Since the 1950s, many upper-ocean species have moved towards the poles by about 52 km every decade. Why move, and what happens to living things and farms on land?
Arctic tundra soils have built up a vast store of carbon. Why is the tundra now giving some back?
Cut down a rainforest and its soil soon fails. If the forest was so rich, where were its riches kept?
Someone planted a shrub to hold a sand dune in place. Why is it now being dug out?
Leave bare rock and a pond untouched in lowland Britain for centuries. Why do both become similar woodland?
atmosphere: In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
Why do so many of the world's hot deserts lie near the same two lines of latitude?
The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?
Air holds water as an invisible gas. What finally squeezes it out as rain?
Weather in the British Isles can swing from gales to frost. What makes it so changeable?
Forecasters can spot a coming gale from a few curved lines on a map. How?
In December 2023 the Panama Canal let through 22 ships a day, against 36 in its "regular scenario". What did a patch of warm Pacific Ocean have to do with it?
Hurricane Ian hit Florida with 130-knot winds in 2022. Why was water, not wind, its deadliest hazard?
Why can a storm cost a rich country billions, yet kill far more people in a poor one?
population: How do you count every person in a country, and how do you know who was missed?
At today's rate, Niger's population would double in about 21 years. Japan's is shrinking. Why?
In 2000, non-communicable diseases caused 58% of the world's deaths. In 2023 they caused 74%. Good news or bad news?
In 1798, Thomas Malthus argued that population would outrun food. Since 1961, the world's population has grown about 2.6 times. Has food per person risen or fallen?
From 1980 China limited most couples to one child. By 2021 it allowed three. Why the U-turn, and can governments change how many children people have?
settlement: In Denmark, 200 people can make a place urban. In Japan it takes 50,000. So how urban is the world?
Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
Why would a city build new homes on old, polluted factory land instead of the empty fields next door?
Northern Ireland has mountains and coasts worth protecting. Why does it still have no National Park?
Some of New York's poorest neighbourhoods lost a quarter of their people in the 1970s. Who moved back in?
In 2011, 1 in 10 people in Mumbai's D ward lived in slums. In M/East ward, more than 3 in 4 did. Why such a gap inside one city?
Dhaka grew from 3 million people in 1980 to over 18 million by 2017. Who gains and who loses when a city grows that fast?
development: Guyana's income per person is more than three and a half times Sri Lanka's. Why do they have exactly the same HDI?
The world halved extreme poverty five years early. So why did it need a new set of goals?
Uganda now gets more money from foreign investors than from aid. Is that good for its development?
BRICS, MINT, "emerging markets": what makes a poorer country's economy take off?
In 1991 India's economy almost stalled. Three decades later it is one of the world's largest. What changed?
plate-tectonics: Coal in Antarctica, fossils across an ocean: what finally proved that continents move?
The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
The same eruption that buries homes can build new land. Is a volcano a hazard or a resource?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?
After a 2004 earthquake off Sumatra, people died in 10 countries around the Indian Ocean. How?
Scientists picked out where a big earthquake seemed overdue. Why couldn't they say when?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
By 2013, Hong Kong said it had cut the landslide risk from its man-made slopes by about 75%. Is preventing disasters worth more than responding to them?
tropical-ecosystems: Rainforest, savanna and desert all lie in the hot tropics. What decides which one grows where?
From the 1960s, irrigation turned Central Asian desert into cotton fields. Later, the Aral Sea largely dried up and fields turned salty. How can watering a desert damage it?
Canals made a dry plain between two Niles into one of Africa's largest irrigation projects. What went wrong next?
Clearing tropical forest and savanna brings farms, jobs and food. Who gains, and what is lost?
Disease wiped out pepper farms in the Amazon in the 1960s. Could farmers rebuild by copying the forest?
dynamic-coastal-environments: Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises out of the sea by about 0.9 m a century. Elsewhere, coasts are drowning. How can both be true?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
Lyme Regis holds back the sea; along the same coast, a road is being let go. Why treat them differently?
climate-change: Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice are up to 800,000 years old. What can they tell us about past climate?
Ice ages came and went for millions of years before humans. What switched them on and off?
Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
How can a ridge of river gravel wind uphill and over hills, when rivers only flow downhill?
County Down's hills look like a basket of eggs. Is that landscape a gift or a problem for the people who live there?
The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?
Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?
In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?
The least developed countries emitted less than 0.4% of all historical fossil CO₂, yet face some of the worst impacts. Who should cut emissions, and who should pay?
cultural-geography: Nearly half of the world's languages are endangered, yet 4 in 10 Londoners were born abroad. Is the world becoming more alike or more diverse?
In Northern Ireland, women in full-time jobs now earn slightly more than men. Has discrimination disappeared?
A hillside with no buildings in sight looks wild. Is it natural, or did people make it what it is?
Only about one person in 27 is an international migrant. Why do some people move while most stay?
Within a year of August 2017, nearly 725,000 people had fled from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Why do so many people flee at once, and what happens where they arrive?
An island lost over half its people in a century. What happens to those who stay?
In 1979 Shenzhen was what its government calls "a small backward border town". By 2024 it had 17.98 million residents. Where did they all come from?
From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?
Swiss voters backed limits on immigration in 2014. What did their government actually do next?
If the internet now spans the globe, why are over two billion people still offline?
In 2025 Access Now recorded at least 313 internet shutdowns. Can citizens win back the freedom to connect?
planning-for-sustainable-settlements: Urban areas use 75% of the world's energy. Vauban, a whole eco-district in Germany, is home to about 5,300 people. Can eco-cities and smart cities make a real difference?
Belfast buries less than one per cent of the rubbish it collects. So why might it run short of room for new homes?
Two neighbouring St Louis estates: one never filled and was torn down; the other stayed full. Why?
Out-of-town shopping parks are easy to drive to. So who loses when one opens?
Belfast needs over thirty thousand new homes by 2035. Where, and how, should it build them?
A giant container ship burns huge amounts of fuel, yet may be the cleanest way to move goods. How?
In 2003 London began charging drivers to enter its centre. By 2007 traffic was still lower, but congestion was back where it started. How?
ethnic-diversity: Two neighbours share a language and a passport. Can they still belong to different ethnic groups?
Nearly half of France's immigrants were born in Africa. How did an empire help make France so diverse?
A square metre of land in Ginza, central Tokyo, is valued at ¥67.1 million. A square metre of housing land in Ome, also in Tokyo, averages ¥98,600. Why the gap?
In parts of Belfast, nine in ten people share one religious background. Why does the city stay divided?
Why do some ethnic tensions end in a peace deal, and others in war or a divided country?
Sri Lanka's civil war ended in 2009 after 26 years. Has the conflict behind it really ended?
tourism: UK residents made about three times as many trips abroad as Indian nationals did in 2025, yet India has about 21 times as many people. Why?
Tourism makes up about a fifth of the Maldives' economy. Yet in 2022 most people working in its resorts were not Maldivian. Who really gains from a resort?
Thailand closed one of its most famous beaches to visitors for about three and a half years. Why would a country shut a beach that tourists love?
Visitors to Mallorca pay a small tax for every day they stay. Has it eased the pressure of mass tourism?
In 2017 Rwanda doubled the price of a permit to see mountain gorillas, to US$1,500. Can making tourism more expensive make it more sustainable?
Ecotourism crosses borders, but no world body can enforce its rules. So who keeps it honest?
